claims.claim: Sort every cell in your body by size, and something odd turns up: each size class weighs roughly the same. (Hook, A4: what a viewer who leaves at second two takes away.)
claims.source_checked: doi:10.1073/pnas.2303077120, full text https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC10523466/fullTextXML; Fig. 3 and 4 images https://cdn.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/blobs/2b19/10523466/a604800d732a/pnas.2303077120fig03.jpg, .../ada6f41502f5/pnas.2303077120fig04.jpg
claims.note: 'Roughly the same' itself is supported: 'a roughly similar fraction of total body mass is present in each logarithmic cell-size class'; Significance calls the inverse relation 'surprising', so 'odd' is fair. What breaks is 'every cell'. The paper did not sort every cell: 'Among the smallest cells, there are breaks in the continuity of the size distribution around platelets and haploid sperm cells, near 10^-11 g. Our size distribution does not include these small cells, and only considers the distribution beginning at red blood cells' (Methods: ignored 'to avoid fitting the distribution over relatively large gaps'). The paper counts platelets as cells (Fig. 1A). Size classes at the gaps would hold nearly nothing, so a viewer who swipes at second two leaves with a claim the source does not make. Line 3 ('the smallest cells it sorted') corrects this only after the hook (A4). Change: drop 'every' and bound the range, e.g. 'Sort the cells in your body by size, from red blood cells up, and something odd turns up: ...'. At the least, drop 'every'.

claims.claim: A twenty twenty-three study combined over fifteen hundred earlier studies to estimate the body's cells, type by type, and sorted them by size.
claims.note: Published online 18 Sep 2023 (PNAS 120(39), 26 Sep 2023). 'with data drawn from >1,500 published sources'; Methods: 'compiles cell size and count data from more than 1,500 published sources for 400 known cell types across 60 tissue systems ... giving 1,264 cell groups'. 'We compile data to estimate cell mass, size range, and cell count', so 'estimate' (not 'count') is right. Cells are binned into size classes (Fig. 3). 'Studies' for 'published sources' is a fair lay paraphrase (the sources include ICRP reference compilations, which are themselves built from studies).

claims.claim: The smallest cells it sorted are red blood cells.
claims.note: 'only considers the distribution beginning at red blood cells (4 x 10^-11 g)'; Methods: bins start 'at the lower bound of erythrocytes'; platelets and the smallest haploid gametes are excluded. 'It sorted' keeps the claim to the binned distribution, which is correct.

claims.claim: The biggest are muscle fibres, more than a million times heavier.
claims.note: 'from a tiny red blood cell to a myocyte, more than a million-fold larger'; sizes 'vary over an enormous seven orders of magnitude from red blood cells to the largest muscle fibers'. Size in the paper is cell mass, so 'heavier' is right. Fig. 3: the largest size classes are made of myocytes. 10^-4 g / 4e-11 g = 2.5 million, so '>1,000,000x' is a floor.

claims.claim: Now put every cell into a size class, each class twice as heavy as the one before.
claims.note: Methods: 'bins increase by a multiplicative factor of 2 from small to large (octave size classes), beginning at the lower bound of erythrocytes, and giving 26 size classes'. 'Every cell' here follows line 3, which has already said where the sorting starts.

claims.claim: Each time the size doubles, there are, on average, about half as many cells.
claims.note: Fig. 3: count per size class regressed on mass, 'slope near -0.97', 95% CI -1.09 to -0.87. Per doubling: 2^-0.97 = 0.51 (CI 0.47 to 0.55), i.e. about half. Fig. 3 shows real bins scattering around the line, so 'on average' is needed and present. The card's 'HALF AS MANY' rounds 0.51, within A3.

claims.claim: So the small cells win on numbers, the big cells win on size, and the two cancel out.
claims.note: 'A slope near -1 implies a roughly inverse relation between cell size and count, such that an increase in size by a given factor is offset by a decrease in cell count by a similar factor'. Count x mass is then about constant per class.

claims.claim: Every class ends up holding roughly the same weight.
claims.note: 'a roughly similar fraction of total body mass is present in each logarithmic cell-size class (Fig. 4A)'; 'cellular biomass is overall approximately evenly spread among cell-size classes'. The very next line gives the exception, as the paper does. 'Roughly' is essential: outside the gap 'all variation in cellular biomass lies within two orders of magnitude' (Fig. 4A bins run from about 10^2 to a few 10^3 g).

claims.claim: SAME WEIGHT
claims.note: The card drops the 'roughly' that the spoken line and the paper both carry. The paper's results say 'roughly similar' and 'approximately evenly spread', with variation of up to two orders of magnitude even outside the gap (Fig. 4A; Fig. 4B male bins range from about 0.2 to 7 kg). A flat 'SAME WEIGHT' overstates this (A6, A3). Change the card to 'ROUGHLY THE SAME WEIGHT' or 'ABOUT THE SAME WEIGHT'.

claims.claim: With one exception: a dip, between the fat cells and the muscle fibres.
claims.note: 'prominent biomass peaks comprising adipocytes (near 10^-6 g) and myocytes (near 10^-4 g), separated by a gap of relatively low biomass'; 'With the exception of this gap, all variation in cellular biomass lies within two orders of magnitude', so 'one exception' is the paper's own framing. (Fig. 4B also shows a low bin near 2x10^-10 g, but the paper names only this gap as the exception.)

claims.claim: In women the dip is smaller, and in a ten-year-old it is fainter still.
claims.note: 'This gap is also evident but less prominent in the reference female, and is even less evident in the 10-y-old reference child (Fig. 4B)'. Fig. 4B agrees. Caveat for the record: the female and child are reference models scaled from the male (myocyte counts held fixed, sizes scaled by muscle-mass ratio 0.625 and 0.393), and the paper has 'greatest confidence' in the male. 'Women' for the paper's representative female is the same level of generalisation as 'a typical man' for the reference male.

claims.claim: Take a typical man. His muscle fibres are fewer than one in fifty thousand of his cells with a nucleus.
claims.note: Fig. 1B caption: skeletal myocytes 'make up <0.002% of the nucleated cell count' (reference male). 0.002% = 1/50,000, and it is an upper bound, so 'fewer than' is right. The reference male (ICRP, 70 kg, 20-50 y) is a fair 'typical man'.

claims.claim: A TYPICAL MAN, sub '70 KG (154 LB)'
claims.note: Reference male 'Male, (70 kg, 176 cm in height and 20 to 50 y of age)'. 70 kg x 2.20462 = 154.3 lb, so 154 lb.

claims.claim: Yet they make up about half the weight of all his cells.
claims.note: Fig. 1B caption: 'Cell biomass is dominated by skeletal myocytes, comprising about half of all 45 kg of cell biomass in the body ... Most of the remaining 23.5 kg ...', i.e. about 21.5 kg = 48%.

claims.claim: And all his cells together weigh about forty-five kilograms.
claims.where: spoken; on-screen: card '45 KG', sub '99 LB'
claims.note: 'all 45 kg of cell biomass in the body' (reference male, Fig. 1B). 45 kg x 2.20462 = 99.2 lb, so 99 lb.

claims.claim: The other twenty-five of his seventy are not cells at all. They are the water, protein and minerals between them.
claims.where: spoken; on-screen: card 'NOT CELLS', sub '25 KG (55 LB)'; card 'BETWEEN THE CELLS'
claims.note: Fig. 2 caption: 'Cell biomass excludes noncellular components of biomass in each tissue, made up of extracellular water, protein, and minerals (~25 kg)'. 45 + 25 = 70 kg, the reference male. 'Between them' = extracellular. 25 kg x 2.20462 = 55.1 lb, so 55 lb.

claims.claim: Sort the life in the ocean by size, as it was before industrial fishing, and most size classes held about the same weight too.
claims.source_checked: doi:10.1126/sciadv.abh3732, full text https://www.ebi.ac.uk/europepmc/webservices/rest/PMC8580314/fullTextXML; Fig. 2 image https://cdn.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/blobs/a00d/8580314/ac12b83f0aa6/sciadv.abh3732-f2.jpg; PNAS paper ref. 44
claims.note: Abstract: 'biomass within most order of magnitude size classes is indeed remarkably constant, near 1 gigatonne (Gt) wet weight (10^15 g), but bacteria and large marine mammals are markedly above and below this value'. This is the 'pristine' state 'before industrial-scale human capture of fish and marine mammals (pre-1850)'. Today 'the upper one-third of the biomass spectrum has been severely truncated', which is why the past tense is right. 'Most' covers the exceptions. 'Too' is supported: the PNAS paper itself links the pattern to 'bodies in the ocean from bacteria to whales (44)'. The ocean classes are tenfold. The line does not claim twofold.

claims.claim: And in your body, nobody knows why. No accepted process explains it yet.
claims.where: spoken; on-screen: cards 'NOBODY KNOWS WHY', 'NOT YET EXPLAINED'
claims.note: Discussion: 'To our knowledge, there is no universally recognized process that accounts for these patterns.' Conclusion: 'the developmental mechanisms underlying this pattern remain unresolved'. The paper offers candidates (random growth processes; mismatched growth and division rates), so 'no accepted process' (not 'no idea at all') is the right reading. Limit: this is the paper's 2023 statement; no later literature was searched to show nothing has since been accepted.

claims.claim: Trillions of tiny cells, far fewer giant ones, and roughly the same weight at every size.
claims.note: '≈36 trillion cells in the male'; non-nucleated blood cells ≈29 trillion (Fig. 1A), so trillions of tiny cells. Skeletal myocytes are <0.002% of nucleated cells (far fewer giant ones). Conclusion: 'cell biomass is roughly independent of cell-size class'. By this point the viewer has heard line 3 (where sorting starts) and line 9 (the dip), so 'roughly ... at every size' matches the paper's own summary.

claims.claim: Chart axis 'CELL MASS IN GRAMS · LOG SCALE' from 10⁻¹¹ to 10⁻² g, marks 'RED BLOOD CELLS / FROM 4 × 10⁻¹¹ g', 'FAT CELLS / ~10⁻⁶ g', 'MUSCLE FIBRES / ~10⁻⁴ g'
claims.note: 'beginning at red blood cells (4 x 10^-11 g)', the lower bound, so 'FROM' is right; 'adipocytes (near 10^-6 g) and myocytes (near 10^-4 g)'. Fig. 3 points: adipocytes around 10^-7 to 10^-6 g, myocytes clustered near 10^-4 g. Size is cell mass in g throughout the paper. The axis range contains all 26 classes (top edge 2.7x10^-3 g).

claims.claim: 26 size classes, each twice the mass of the last, starting at 4 × 10⁻¹¹ g
claims.note: Methods: factor-2 bins 'beginning at the lower bound of erythrocytes, and giving 26 size classes'. 4e-11 x 2^26 = 2.68e-3 g, matching Fig. 3's last bin.

claims.claim: Bars 'NUMBER OF CELLS · LOG SCALE · SCHEMATIC': a straight falling staircase
claims.note: Fig. 3's bins fall along the fitted slope -0.97 over about 13 orders of magnitude in count, with scatter (including a sag near 10^-5 g) that a straight staircase leaves out. Labelled log scale and schematic (A6), so it shows the fitted trend without claiming bin-by-bin data. The dip is shown in the next chart.

claims.claim: Bars 'WEIGHT IN EACH CLASS · LOG SCALE · SCHEMATIC': roughly level, with a dip between the fat and muscle marks
claims.note: Fig. 4A (log biomass axis): bins roughly level at 10^2 to 10^3 g with a low stretch between the adipocyte (~10^-6 g) and myocyte (~10^-4 g) peaks. The small peaks either side of the gap are flattened, which is acceptable on a log-scale schematic that says so.

claims.claim: Three stacked rows of level bars 'MAN', 'WOMAN', 'CHILD, 10', titled 'WEIGHT IN EACH CLASS · SCHEMATIC'; the dip is shallower in each row down
claims.note: The order of dip depth (man > woman > child) matches the text and Fig. 4B. But this title, unlike the previous chart's, drops 'LOG SCALE', so a viewer reads the bars as linear. The paper's man/woman/child comparison (Fig. 4B) is on linear axes, and there the bins are not level: they range from about 0.2 to 7 kg, with two tall peaks (fat, muscle) either side of the dip. Level bars on an unstated scale misrepresent that panel (A6). Change: add 'LOG SCALE' to the title ('WEIGHT IN EACH CLASS · LOG SCALE · SCHEMATIC'), or, if the rows stay linear, draw the fat and muscle peaks.

claims.claim: Grid of 250 × 200 dots captioned '50,000 CELLS WITH A NUCLEUS · FEWER THAN 1 MUSCLE FIBRE', one dot ringed
claims.note: 250 x 200 = 50,000. '<0.002% of the nucleated cell count' means fewer than 1 per 50,000. The ringed dot pictures the upper bound, and the caption's 'FEWER THAN 1' keeps it accurate.

claims.claim: Bar 'ALL HIS CELLS · 45 KG', half filled 'MUSCLE FIBRES ≈ HALF'; extends with 'NOT CELLS · 25 KG', '70 KG MAN', 'WATER · PROTEIN · MINERALS'; lengths 45:25
claims.note: 45 kg cell biomass, myocytes 'about half' (~21.5 kg = 48%), noncellular 'extracellular water, protein, and minerals (~25 kg)', 45 + 25 = 70 kg reference male. The 45:25 proportions match.

claims.claim: Ocean card: axis 'SIZE OF SEA LIFE, BACTERIA TO WHALES · LOG SCALE', level bars titled 'BEFORE INDUSTRIAL FISHING · SCHEMATIC', first two bars higher and last two lower
claims.note: Fig. 2 ('The pristine ocean biomass spectrum ... approximately 1 Gt ... with exceptions at either extreme'). Upper 200 m: the two smallest (bacteria) bins sit at about 2.5 Gt, middle bins near 1 Gt, and the two marine-mammal bins at about 0.1 and 0.06 Gt. The axis spans bacteria to whales. Pre-1850 = before industrial fishing and whaling. Labelled schematic.
